subject: Aurora CarePilot — Dedicated GPU entitlement & burst resilience model

Subject: Aurora CarePilot — Dedicated GPU entitlement & burst resilience model

Hi Marco / Aurora ops team,

Thanks again for the time on Friday. As promised I'm sending our preliminary sizing and a few requests so we can converge on a committed capacity recommendation that meets your p95 latency SLO and operational burst needs. Attached: aurora_mrp_token_profile.csv (your sample traffic) and an initial-sim-params.pdf with the assumptions we used.

Quick summary of what we modeled:
- Workload: CarePilot inference requests (single-turn prompts, avg response 140 tokens).
- Target SLO: p95 tail latency <= 350ms for interactive routing.
- Peak burst shape: 3-minute peaks, concurrency spikes up to 220 concurrent requests.
- Models: we evaluated two serving variants — "CP-4q" (4-bit quantized, KV-cache friendly) and "CP-16" (16-bit float).

Key numbers (ballpark):
- CP-4q per A100-80GB: ~420 tokens/sec sustained (mixed batch, 16-token avg batch) and ~320 tokens/sec under 95th percentile latency conditions.
- CP-16 per A100-80GB: ~150 tokens/sec sustained; p95 latency hit at scale.

Sizing takeaway (preliminary):
- Committed pool recommendation: 10 A100-80GB GPUs running CP-4q to meet typical sustained volume with a 1.4x safety factor.
- Burst capacity (on-demand or protected reserve): additional 8 GPUs available for 3–10 minute peaks to keep p95 under 350ms across the burst window.

Open asks from Aurora to finalize:
1) Confirm your expected average request length and any planned increase in system prompts or tool-calls that add tokens.
2) Confirm acceptable failure modes if the pool is saturated (queueing vs graceful degradation vs fallback to smaller model).
3) Any regulatory constraints around private deployment vs hosted (affects where burst capacity can be sourced).

If you want we can run a short stochastic simulation against your CSV profile with a safety multiplier you pick — I included an example run in the sim params file.

Next step: if you give the green light we’ll run the sim with your 1-week production export and return a time-series of expected p95, tokens/sec, and an ops playbook for burst handling.

Best,
Vanessa Ortiz
Head of Strategic Accounts, Redwood Inference
Redwood Inference

Attachment(s): aurora_mrp_token_profile.csv (csv), initial-sim-params.pdf (pdf)

Vanessa, thanks for this — very helpful. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Average request payload: ~110 tokens in, ~140 tokens out (total ~250 tokens per request). We included a few long-form summaries in the sample export — those are 600–1,200 token responses but rare (~1% of requests).
- Burst behavior: our clinical triage windows (08:00–09:00 local) can produce multi-minute spikes as multiple clinics warm up. Peak concurrency estimate is 200–250 RPS, but those sessions are short (1–3 requests/session).
- Failover: prefer graceful degradation — fall back to CP-16 (lower quality) if CP-4q pool is saturated, before rejecting. We'd like a brief runbook for the sequence.

A couple of asks:
1) Can you show the effect of the 1% long responses on p95 if they coincide with a peak?
2) What latency variance should we budget for cold-started KV caches after autoscaling?

Looping in ops@ to confirm no regulatory blocks to using hosted burst capacity in the us-east region; if there is a problem we’ll need the burst to be private-only.

—Marco
Marco Rossi

Subject: RE: Aurora CarePilot — Dedicated GPU entitlement & burst resilience model (sim results)

Vanessa / Marco / team — attaching carepilot-sim-results.xlsx with the stochastic runs. Highlights below: 

1) Baseline per-GPU throughput (CP-4q on A100-80GB) we measured under our test harness:
   - median sustained: 430 tokens/sec
   - 95th-percentile under moderate QoS pressure: 315 tokens/sec
   - cold-warmup (first 90s after scale-up) p95 latency multiplier: ~1.45x compared to steady-state (kv warming and batching ramp).

2) Long-tail events impact: the 1% requests >600 tokens pushes effective tokens/sec demand by ~12% during the event window and increases p95 by ~18–25% if concurrency is high and burst buffer is insufficient. We recommend modeling a 1.25x token multiplier for safety when there are rare large outputs.

3) Recommended capacity (detailed in sheet):
   - Committed pool: 9 A100-80GB GPUs running CP-4q (this meets typical weekday sustained demand with 1.2x buffer).
   - Short-duration burst reserve: 10 A100-80GB (either warm standby in their private deployment or hosted burst in us-east), which covers simulated 3–10 minute peaks with p95 < 350ms when used.
   - Fallback path: CP-4q -> CP-16 auto-fallback (same pool tag) -> degrade non-critical augmentations (rich system prompt truncation).

4) Autoscale and pre-warm guidance:
   - Staged join: onboard new GPU nodes to serving pool in a staggered 15–20s cadence to avoid KV stampedes.
   - Preheat strategy: proactively load KV and a 2-minute synthetic traffic ramp to reduce cold-warm p95 multiplier from 1.45x to ~1.12x. This costs token-equivalent overhead (we estimate 8–12% extra token usage during preheat windows).

5) Operational playbook (high level):
   - On detection of rising concurrency > 75% of committed capacity for >60s: trigger staged warmup of 2 GPUs and notify SRE.
   - If concurrency persists beyond 3 minutes and p95 > 300ms: bring burst reserve to active and enable fallback policy.
   - Post-burst: drain queued requests and run cache reconciliation job for 90s to stabilize p95.

I attached the sim workbook and included the key time-series we ran against Marco's CSV. Let me know if Aurora wants a live run with their 7-day raw export — we can produce an annotated runbook that maps to billing commit tiers.

Regards,
Priyom Das
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
